# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading: "Two Years On" Follow-up (Protocol VC-2023-04-F)

This report directly addresses the three questions the earlier documents left open: durability, mechanism, and unrecorded hours.

- The mediation analysis was registered before outcomes were available.
- A log-based hours measure was added to catch unrecorded work.
- The comparison of decay over time is like-for-like.
- The authors are candid about the weakness of the Halden survivor data and of the control-office "meeting audit".

Its main conclusions are reasonable: the per-hour gain declined but persisted at 24 months, and the meetings pathway is supported. But several details need scrutiny:

- what the log measure actually captures
- where the baseline meetings data came from
- control-group contamination that affects the size of the decline
- the precision of the mediation estimates

## Arithmetic

| Figure | Check |
|---|---|
| Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Logs: 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden 11: 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% ✓ (34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4% ✓) |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |
| Decline on timesheet measure | 12.5 → 9.8, about −22% relative ("about a quarter", slightly generous) |

## What the report does well

- **The mediation was registered at month 11,** before 24-month outcomes were known. That is a genuine confirmatory test of a hypothesis generated in the exploratory analysis.
- **The decay comparison is like-for-like.** The authors use timesheet hours at both 9 and 24 months (12.5% → 9.8%). Comparing 12.5% with the stricter log figure of 8.5% would have overstated the decline.
- **It checks the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies.** It finds all four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the concern that the "no sign of decay" claim rested on the weakest designs.
- **The counter arm comparison is now controlled.** Waiting time is reported against control offices (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes), unlike the nine-month report's treated-only before/after figure.
- **The Halden data are described honestly.** The authors call the subset "survivors twice over" and decline to generalise from it.
- **It doesn't overclaim from the meeting audit.** The report says plainly that it can't tell whether reorganisation alone would capture the gain.

## Problems

### 1. What does the log measure capture?

The log measure is described as "active log-in time on the case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". If it records only case work, it excludes meetings, and the numbers don't fit:

- **Baseline:** about 37.9 timesheet hours minus 7.4 meeting hours leaves roughly 30.5 hours of non-meeting time.
- **Month 24:** treated timesheet hours fell about 12% to roughly 33.4, and meetings fell to 3.9, leaving roughly 29.5 hours.
- **Implication:** non-meeting time fell only about 3%, yet logs are reported as falling 11%.

There are two ways to resolve this:

- **Logs capture total working time** (logged in but not necessarily active on cases, including during meetings). Then "active" is misleading, but the hours comparison stands.
- **Logs capture case work only.** Then the −11% conflicts with the meetings data. And if case-work time fell only about 3% while output fell 3.4%, output per hour *of case work* barely changed. In that case the entire "per-hour gain" would be time moved out of meetings. That is consistent with the mediation result, but it is a different and sharper conclusion than the paper draws.

The definition matters for interpreting both the hours correction and the mediation. It should be stated precisely.

### 2. Where did the baseline meetings data come from?

The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, at managers' request, and were not part of the plan. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 hours (treated) and 7.2 hours (control). Presumably these were retrieved retrospectively from calendar systems, which is plausible. The report should say so, and confirm the baseline and month-24 data were extracted the same way.

### 3. Control contamination affects the decay estimate

Two of seven control offices cut meetings in month 15 and saw about 4.1% higher output per hour afterwards. Averaged across seven offices, that is roughly a 1.2% rise in control productivity over part of the window. Any improvement in control offices shrinks the treated-minus-control difference. So:

- part of the 12.5% → 9.8% "decline" may be the control group improving, not the treatment effect fading
- the 24-month effect may be slightly *understated*

The report treats the meeting audit only as evidence about reorganisation without an hours cut. It doesn't connect it to the decay estimate.

A related oddity: control-office meetings averaged 7.2 → 7.0. If two offices fell 2.1 hours each, the other five must have risen by about 0.5 hours on average. That is possible (drift, or timing of the month-24 snapshot), but worth a note.

### 4. The decline is not itself statistically established

The 9-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 and +4.6 to +15.2. "Consistent with some fading" is a fair description, but so is "no clear change". With two time points, the trajectory is unknown. A linear trend from 12.5% to 9.8% would reach zero only after several more years, but there's no basis for assuming linearity in either direction. Monthly or quarterly estimates would help.

### 5. The mediation estimates are probably too precise

- **Effective sample size.** There are 14 clusters (7 v 7). "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but they aren't independent within offices, so the effective sample is closer to 14. Intervals like 28–66% may be optimistic unless inference accounts for clustering with few clusters.
- **Unmeasured confounding.** Mediators aren't randomised. Offices with stronger managers may cut more meetings *and* improve output for other reasons. The authors acknowledge this.
- **Interacting mediators.** Fewer meetings could reduce fatigue, so additive shares (47% + 18%) assume more separation than may exist.
- **Partly by construction.** If output per hour counts meeting hours in the denominator, cutting unproductive meeting time raises output per hour almost by definition. That *is* the mechanism, not an artifact. But it means "meetings explain 47%" is close to saying the gain comes from removing unproductive time. It is less a claim about working faster.

### 6. "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the evidence

The reverted marketing agency cited *client deadlines*. In the Halden pilot and the meta-analysis's coding, marketing counts as discretionary work. One of the three reversions therefore came from a discretionary setting. The summary's framing makes the coverage-bound/discretionary split look cleaner than the data show.

### 7. The Halden survivor estimate has further caveats

- **Response selection.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. Non-response adds a third layer of selection on top of completing the pilot and choosing to continue.
- **Possibly mismatched baseline.** The 40.3-hour baseline appears to be the average of the 27 time-tracking organisations, not of these 11. Their own baseline should be used.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** With no comparison group, two years of business growth, technology change or economic conditions could move output in either direction. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate.

### 8. Smaller points

- **Quality and wellbeing outcomes.** Appeal overturn rates and resignations are still reported as levels without intervals. Sick days (−27%) have no CI.
- **Cost of the counter arm.** The +9% cost per contact sits oddly with 12% more staff at full pay. The calculation should be shown.
- **Cost of the case-processing arm.** It is still not reported. With output per FTE at −3.4% at full pay, unit labour cost rose by roughly 3.5%, before any overtime.
- **Authorship.** The authors are evaluating, in part, their own earlier hypothesis, and a Halden author is evaluating Halden. The registration mitigates this. But the framing of critics ("since dismissed as post hoc") reads as somewhat vindicatory.

## How it bears on the earlier documents

| Question | Before this report | After |
|---|---|---|
| Is the per-hour gain an artifact? | Corrected estimates about 8–12%, short follow-up | 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) at 24 months on the strictest hours measure, randomised. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported |
| Does it decay? | Meta-analysis said no, using 4 weak studies | Modest decline in the one controlled long study, possibly partly control-group improvement. Not significant, not zero |
| Mechanism? | Meetings exploratory; fatigue assumed | Meetings about half, fatigue under a fifth, under strong assumptions with 14 clusters |
| Coverage-bound work? | Output per worker about −9 to −11% | The county ended it: waits nearly doubled, and restoring service cost about 9% more per contact |
| Sector-general? | Doubtful | Not supported. The two Halden retail/hospitality reverters fit the coverage-bound pattern |

## Bottom line

In discretionary, backlog-type public-sector work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a durable gain of about 8–10% in output per actual hour over two years. Output per employee ended slightly below control (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2). Roughly half the gain appears to come from removing low-value meeting time.

Two questions remain open:

- **Could the gain be had without cutting hours?** The control-office meeting audit hints yes, but no arm tested reorganisation alone. That is the obvious next trial, and it would settle whether the hours cut is the active ingredient or just the trigger.
- **What does it cost?** Total cost has never been reported.

The meaning of the log-hours measure also needs clarifying. If it captures case work only, the conclusion shifts further: nearly all of the measured gain would be time moved out of meetings.
